subject: dynamic occupancy model for Marsh Seedeater

messages.author: aa17a960edc5c28f
messages.subject: dynamic occupancy model for Marsh Seedeater
parts:
Hi Marc and all, last year I asked you advice on assessing habitat variables that affect occupancy of an endangered bird species Marsh Seedeater. I had about 100 sites (points), 20% were presences from the first season. I repeated the survey last december (second season), visiting each point about 3 or 4 times. So the first season I do not have repeated visits, but the second season I do have. In each season I measured 3 habitat variables (e.g. grass heigh, number of trees, seed -food- abundance) that may govern extinction and colonization rates. 

So, as I understand, I can estimate occupancy for both seasons, correcting for imperfect detection. Then I should adjust a dynamic occupancy model with covariates that allow me to assess if the change in covariates levels are affecting colonization/extinction rates. Some sites might be correlated, and temporal correlation may also exist so I guess random effects would be good to include in the model. 

So the question is if you know a example that I can follow for applying this model, with the code and results interpretation and plotting.

Thank you very much in advanced. 

Joaquín. 

--

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: AW: dynamic occupancy model for Marsh Seedeater
parts:
Dear Joaquin,

 

You have only a single visit in the first year, so you have no direct way of estimating detection separately from occurrence in that year. However, if you can make and are willing to make the assumption that p is comparable in year 1 and 2, then you can fit the model anyway. (Making this assumption is what 90% or so of people in ecology do. I am not saying that it is a good thing necessarily, but at least, you should not necessarily be slayed for this).

 

You could fit a model with the data from each year stacked, treat year as a factor and use occu() in unmarked and this would give you estimates for each year, but in general I think that it may often be more interesting to look at the two parameters that govern the dynamics underlying any change in occupancy state and how these are affected by any covariates. So I think that the dynocc model may also be interesting for your case. But that is really for you to decide.

 

Best regards  --- Marc

messages.author: 527d9b3ec7deff2d
messages.subject: Re: dynamic occupancy model for Marsh Seedeater
parts:
For what it's worth, I had a study using a dynamic occupancy model with only 2 years of data and no repeat surveys in year 1:

http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ece3.1618/full

The inferences can certainly change even with only 1 additional year of data, though obviously you have to temper conclusions because of sample size and uncertainty.  I argued that a Bayesian approach was particularly useful there but probably oversold it.  Given the multiple states I couldn't use unmarked either way (PRESENCE would likely have worked).
